There are many historical and contemporary claims of superlative height for species beyond those listed in the table above. For example, several articles published in 1878 describe an *[Eucalyptus amygdalina](/wiki/Eucalyptus_amygdalina "Eucalyptus amygdalina")* exceeding 380 feet (120 m) and others nearing 420 feet (130 m) up to 500 feet (150 m), including the [Nooksack Giant](/wiki/Nooksack_Giant "Nooksack Giant") which was measured using a tape at 465 feet (142 m) after being cut down.[[56]](#cite_note-57)[[57]](#cite_note-58)[[58]](#cite_note-59)

The heights of the tallest trees in the world have been the subject of considerable dispute and much exaggeration. Modern verified measurements with [laser rangefinders](/wiki/Laser_rangefinder "Laser rangefinder") or with [tape](/wiki/Measuring_tape "Measuring tape") drop measurements made by tree climbers (such as those carried out by canopy researchers), have shown that some older [tree height measurement](/wiki/Tree_height_measurement "Tree height measurement") methods are often unreliable, sometimes producing exaggerations of 5% to 15% or more above the real height.[[59]](#cite_note-60)

Spurred on by a franchise-record 13-game winning streak in October and November, the Devils finished third in the entire league and set a franchise record for wins (52) and points (112). The team's climb from 63 points the prior season to 112 points marked the largest single-season increase by any NHL team in an 82-game season. [![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/Parthenon_restoration.gif/250px-Parthenon_restoration.gif)](/wiki/File:Parthenon_restoration.gif)

Animation showing the Parthenon in 2011 and how it looked originally

In the mid-5th century BC, when the Athenian Acropolis became the seat of the [Delian League](/wiki/Delian_League "Delian League"), [Pericles](/wiki/Pericles "Pericles") initiated the building project that lasted the entire second half of the century. The most important buildings visible on the Acropolis today – the Parthenon, the [Propylaia](/wiki/Propylaia_(Acropolis_of_Athens) "Propylaia (Acropolis of Athens)"), the [Erechtheion](/wiki/Erechtheion "Erechtheion") and the temple of [Athena Nike](/wiki/Athena_Nike "Athena Nike") – were erected during this period. The Parthenon was built under the general supervision of [Phidias](/wiki/Phidias "Phidias"), who also had charge of the sculptural decoration. The architects [Ictinos](/wiki/Ictinos "Ictinos") and [Callicrates](/wiki/Callicrates "Callicrates") began their work in 447, and the building was substantially completed by 432. Work on the decorations continued until at least 431.[[62]](#cite_note-62)

The Parthenon was built primarily by men who knew how to work marble. These quarrymen had exceptional skills and were able to cut the blocks of marble to very specific measurements. The quarrymen also knew how to avoid the faults, which were numerous in the [Pentelic marble](/wiki/Pentelic_marble "Pentelic marble"). If the marble blocks were not up to standard, the architects would reject them. The marble was worked with iron tools – picks, points, punches, chisels, and drills. The quarrymen would hold their tools against the marble block and firmly tap the surface of the rock.[[63]](#cite_note-auto-63)

Brooklyn Technical

Main article: [Brooklyn Technical High School](/wiki/Brooklyn_Technical_High_School "Brooklyn Technical High School")

One of the original three specialized high schools in New York City (the other two being Stuyvesant High School and Bronx High School of Science). In 1918, Dr. Albert L. Colston, chair of the Math Department at Manual Training High School, recommended establishing a technical high school for Brooklyn boys. His plan envisioned a heavy concentration of [math](/wiki/Math "Math"), science, and [drafting](/wiki/Technical_drawing "Technical drawing") courses with parallel paths leading either to college or to a technical career in industry. By 1922, Dr. Colston's concept was approved by the Board of Education, and Brooklyn Technical High School opened in a converted warehouse at 49 Flatbush Avenue Extension, with 2,400 students. This location, in the shadow of the [Manhattan Bridge](/wiki/Manhattan_Bridge "Manhattan Bridge"), is the reason the school seal bears the image of this bridge, rather than the [Brooklyn Bridge](/wiki/Brooklyn_Bridge "Brooklyn Bridge"). Brooklyn Tech would occupy one more location before settling into its current site, for which the groundbreaking was held in 1930.
